essays.stem: Explain the steps a person should take to set up a new salon legally in Jamaica, including registration and tax numbers.
essays.modelAnswer: First she decides on the type of business, such as a sole trader, a partnership or a limited company. She registers the business name, or forms the company, at the Companies Office of Jamaica. She makes sure she and the business have a TRN from Tax Administration Jamaica (TAJ). She finds out from TAJ whether the salon's expected taxable sales will pass the GCT threshold, and registers for GCT if they do. If she will employ staff, she registers as an employer so she can deduct and pay over PAYE income tax, NIS, NHT and Education Tax, and she collects each worker's TRN and NIS number. She also checks other rules, such as a public health inspection of the salon, fire safety and any approval needed from the local municipal corporation for the building or signs. She opens a separate business bank account and sets up a simple record-keeping system. Because rules and figures change, she should check the current rules with TAJ and the other offices, and get advice from an accountant.
markingPoints: Chooses a business type and registers the name or company with the Companies Office of Jamaica
Gets a TRN from TAJ
Checks the GCT threshold and registers for GCT if needed
Registers as an employer and collects workers' TRN and NIS numbers if employing staff
Checks other rules (health, fire, local), sets up a bank account and records, and checks current rules with TAJ

essays.stem: Explain when a salon must register for GCT, and what it must do once it is registered.
essays.modelAnswer: General Consumption Tax (GCT) is a tax on the sale of many goods and services in Jamaica. A salon must register for GCT when its taxable sales pass the threshold set by law over a period. The threshold and the rate can change, so the owner must check the current rules with Tax Administration Jamaica (TAJ) and keep an eye on her sales. Once registered, the salon must charge GCT at the current rate on its taxable services and products, and give proper receipts or invoices. The GCT collected belongs to the government, so it should be kept separate and not spent. The salon must file a GCT return by each due date TAJ sets, even in a month with few or no sales, and pay over the GCT owed. It can usually claim a credit for GCT it paid on business purchases, but only with valid tax invoices. It must keep all sales and purchase records so it can show how the figures were worked out.
markingPoints: Registration is required when taxable sales pass the threshold; check the current figures with TAJ
Charges GCT at the current rate and gives proper receipts or invoices
Keeps GCT collected separate, as it is government money
Files returns and pays by each due date, even in slow months
Claims credits only with valid tax invoices and keeps records

essays.stem: Describe the records and receipts a salon should keep, and how to keep them in good order.
essays.modelAnswer: A salon should keep a record of all money coming in, such as daily sales of services and products, with copies of the receipts given to clients and card machine slips. It should keep records of money going out, such as supplier invoices and receipts for stock, rent, electricity, water, phone and equipment. Bank statements and deposit slips show what went in and out of the bank. If it has employees, it keeps payroll records: each worker's pay, deductions, payslips and the amounts paid over to TAJ. GCT records and copies of all tax returns are also kept. To keep them in good order, the owner writes up the cash book every day or week, files receipts by month in labelled folders or scans them, and backs up computer records. She checks the cash book against the bank statement each month. Records are stored safely, away from damp and fire, for as long as TAJ requires, so the owner should check the current rules.
markingPoints: Income records: sales, receipts, card slips
Spending records: supplier invoices and receipts for costs
Bank statements, payroll records, GCT records and copies of returns
Keeps them up to date and filed by date, with backups
Reconciles with the bank, stores safely and keeps them as long as TAJ requires

essays.stem: Explain the four statutory deductions from an employee's pay in Jamaica, what each one is for, and the employer's duties.
essays.modelAnswer: The four statutory deductions are PAYE income tax, NIS, NHT and Education Tax. PAYE (Pay As You Earn) is income tax taken from wages each payday, when pay is above the tax-free level. NIS (National Insurance Scheme) contributions give workers benefits such as a pension in later life and help after an injury at work. NHT (National Housing Trust) contributions help workers to get housing loans. Education Tax helps to pay for education in Jamaica. The employer must get each worker's TRN and NIS number, and work out each deduction correctly at the current rates, which she checks with Tax Administration Jamaica (TAJ). She takes the deductions from the worker's pay and adds the employer's own share of NIS, NHT and Education Tax, plus any other employer contributions the law requires. She pays the total over to TAJ and files the returns by the due dates. She gives each worker a payslip showing gross pay, each deduction and net pay, and keeps payroll records.
markingPoints: Names all four: PAYE income tax, NIS, NHT and Education Tax
Says what each is for (income tax, social security benefits, housing, education)
Collects TRN and NIS numbers and works out deductions at current rates checked with TAJ
Adds the employer's share and pays over to TAJ, filing by the due dates
Gives payslips and keeps payroll records

essays.stem: A stylist rents a chair in a salon and works for herself. Explain her own tax and record-keeping duties, and how they differ from those of a stylist employed by the salon.
essays.modelAnswer: A self-employed stylist runs her own small business. She needs her own TRN. She must keep records of all the money she earns from clients and all her business costs, such as chair rent, products and tools, with receipts. Each year she must file an income tax return with Tax Administration Jamaica (TAJ) and pay income tax on her profit, making any advance payments TAJ requires. Self-employed people also pay their own contributions, such as NIS, NHT and Education Tax. If her own taxable sales pass the GCT threshold, she must register for GCT. She must check the current rules and due dates with TAJ. An employed stylist is different. Her employer deducts PAYE income tax, NIS, NHT and Education Tax from her pay, adds the employer's share and pays it to TAJ. The employed stylist does not keep business records, but she should check her payslips and keep them. So the self-employed stylist has much more responsibility for her own tax.
markingPoints: Self-employed: own TRN and full records of income and costs with receipts
Files her own income tax return and pays tax on profit by the due dates
Pays her own contributions (NIS, NHT, Education Tax) and registers for GCT if over the threshold
Employed: the employer deducts and pays over PAYE, NIS, NHT and Education Tax
States that the self-employed stylist carries more responsibility and should check rules with TAJ

essays.stem: Explain the risks to a salon owner of not complying with tax rules, and the benefits of complying.
essays.modelAnswer: If a salon owner does not file returns or pay tax on time, she may have to pay penalties and interest, which can grow into a large debt. Tax Administration Jamaica (TAJ) can take action to collect money owed. Leaving sales out of records or keeping deductions that belong to workers is against the law and can lead to serious legal trouble. Workers may lose benefits, such as NIS pension credits or NHT contributions, if the employer does not pay over their deductions, which harms them and damages trust. Without a Tax Compliance Certificate, the salon may not be able to do some business, such as getting certain licences or contracts. Complying has many benefits. The owner avoids penalties and stress, and can get a TCC when it is needed. Good records help her see how the business is doing and make better decisions. Banks are more likely to lend to a business with proper accounts. Staff trust an employer who pays their deductions, and the salon builds a good name.
markingPoints: Risk: penalties, interest and collection action
Risk: legal trouble for evasion or keeping workers' deductions
Risk: workers lose benefits and trust is damaged; no TCC for some business
Benefit: no penalties, TCC available, good records for decisions
Benefit: easier to get loans, and trust from staff and clients

essays.stem: Describe how a salon owner can stay up to date with changes to tax and business rules.
essays.modelAnswer: Tax rates, thresholds and rules can change, often in the yearly budget, so the owner must not rely on what she learned years ago. The most reliable source is Tax Administration Jamaica (TAJ), through its website, its offices and its notices. She can sign up for any updates TAJ offers and read official notices carefully. For business registration she can check with the Companies Office of Jamaica, and for minimum wage and staff matters with the Ministry of Labour and Social Security. She can read the news, especially around budget time, but should check any news against the official source. An accountant or tax adviser can explain changes and how they affect the salon. Business groups and training courses also share information. The owner should keep a compliance calendar and update it when rules change, and set reminders on her phone. Whenever she is not sure, she should check the current rules with TAJ before acting.
markingPoints: Understands that rules and rates change (for example in the budget)
Uses TAJ as the main source (website, offices, notices or updates)
Uses other official sources: Companies Office, Ministry of Labour
Uses an accountant, business groups or news checked against official sources
Keeps a compliance calendar with reminders and checks with TAJ when unsure

essays.stem: Describe how to set up a compliance calendar for a small salon, and what it should include.
essays.modelAnswer: A compliance calendar is a plan of every tax and legal task the salon must do and when. First the owner lists all her duties, checking each one with Tax Administration Jamaica (TAJ) or her accountant. These include monthly tasks, such as paying over payroll deductions and filing payroll returns, and filing GCT returns and paying GCT if the salon is registered. Yearly tasks include filing the income tax return, any yearly payroll return, renewing business registrations or company annual returns, and renewing any permits or inspections, such as public health and fire. She writes each task on a wall calendar or in a phone calendar on its due date, as TAJ or the other office sets it, and adds a reminder a week or more before so there is time to prepare. She notes who is responsible for each task and where the records are kept. She ticks off each task when done and keeps proof, such as receipts for payments. She reviews the calendar whenever rules change.
markingPoints: Lists all duties, checking with TAJ or an accountant
Includes monthly tasks: payroll deductions and returns, and GCT if registered
Includes yearly tasks: income tax return, registrations and permits
Uses a calendar with due dates and early reminders, and names who is responsible
Ticks off tasks, keeps proof and updates the calendar when rules change

essays.stem: Apart from tax, describe other rules a salon in Jamaica must follow, such as health, safety, consumer and staff rules.
essays.modelAnswer: A salon must keep high standards of hygiene, because the local public health department may inspect it. Tools must be cleaned and disinfected, single-use items used once, and towels changed for each client. It must have clean water, proper waste disposal and a sharps box. For safety, the salon keeps fire extinguishers checked, exits clear and wiring safe, and follows fire safety advice. Chemicals are stored and used as the maker's instructions say, with safety data sheets and first aid at hand. Consumer rules mean prices must be clear, products must not be described falsely, and clients get receipts and fair treatment of complaints. Client information on record cards must be kept private under the privacy law. For staff, the salon must pay at least the national minimum wage, give fair hours, holidays and leave as the law requires, and treat workers without discrimination. The owner should check the current rules with the health department, the fire service, the Ministry of Labour and other official offices.
markingPoints: Health and hygiene rules, with public health inspection
Fire and general safety, including safe storage of chemicals
Consumer rules: clear prices, honest descriptions, receipts, complaints
Privacy of client information
Staff rules: minimum wage, hours and leave, no discrimination; checks with official offices

essays.stem: Explain why a salon owner should be honest in all tax matters, and what she should do if she finds a mistake in a return she has already filed.
essays.modelAnswer: Being honest in tax matters is the law, and it is also fair. Taxes pay for public services such as schools, hospitals and roads that the salon, its staff and its clients use. Deductions taken from workers' pay are their money held for them, so keeping them is like stealing from staff. Hiding sales or making up costs is tax evasion, which can lead to large penalties and legal action, and it can destroy the salon's good name. Honest records also give the owner a true picture of her business. If she finds a mistake in a return she has already filed, she should act quickly and not hide it. She should check the figures and her records, and ask her accountant for help if needed. Then she should contact Tax Administration Jamaica (TAJ) to correct the return in the way TAJ requires, and pay any extra tax owed, with any interest. Owning up early is usually treated better than being found out later.
markingPoints: Honesty is the law and is fair; taxes pay for public services
Workers' deductions are their money and must be paid over
Dishonesty (evasion) leads to penalties, legal action and loss of good name
For a mistake: act quickly, check records, get help from an accountant
Contacts TAJ to correct the return and pays any amount owed

practical1.title: Make a start-up compliance checklist and a 12-month compliance calendar for a new salon
practical1.brief: As a group, prepare the compliance papers for a new salon and spa. The assessor gives you a scenario card (for example: 'Natural Roots Salon and Spa' opening in Spanish Town, owned by one person, with three employees, one stylist who rents a chair and works for herself, retail product sales, and expected sales that may pass the GCT threshold). Give each member one area to research and lead: (a) registering the business; (b) the TRN and GCT; (c) employer duties and the four statutory deductions (PAYE income tax, NIS, NHT and Education Tax); (d) records and receipts; (e) other rules, such as public health, fire safety, consumer rules, client privacy and minimum wage. Use the information pack the assessor gives you or official websites on a Centre computer (Tax Administration Jamaica, the Companies Office of Jamaica and the Ministry of Labour and Social Security). Do not state figures or rates you have not checked: write 'check the current rules with Tax Administration Jamaica' instead. In stages: (1) make a start-up checklist showing each task, which office deals with it and the documents needed; (2) make a 12-month compliance calendar on chart paper showing monthly and yearly tasks, with reminders; (3) make a poster for the staff room: 'Our tax and legal duties'; (4) present the checklist, calendar and poster to the assessor, with each member explaining their area. Photograph each stage and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: A scenario card and an information pack from the assessor
A Centre computer with internet access to official websites (if available)
Blank checklist sheets, chart paper, markers and a ruler
A phone or camera for photos
photos: Each member's research notes for their area, with the source written on them
The 12-month compliance calendar with monthly and yearly tasks
The group presenting to the assessor (papers and charts only)
The final papers, with any corrections the assessor asked for
checklist: Found correct information for their area from an official or reliable source, and noted the source
Named the right office for each task (TAJ, Companies Office, Ministry of Labour, health department)
Correctly listed the four statutory deductions and the employer's duty to pay them over to TAJ
Stated GCT registration correctly: only when taxable sales pass the threshold, with no made-up figures
Put tasks in the calendar sensibly, with 'check the due date with TAJ' where not sure
Explained their area clearly and correctly to the assessor
Included record-keeping and other salon rules in the papers
Worked well with the group and checked others' work
safety: Use only official or reliable websites; do not download files or enter any personal details
Use only the made-up names and numbers on the scenario card; never write a real TRN
At the computer, sit with good posture, keep cables tidy and take short breaks
Keep the work area tidy, with bags and chairs out of the walkways

practical2.title: Keep a week's business records and prepare payslips and a payroll summary
practical2.brief: As a group, keep one week's records for a small salon and prepare its payroll. The assessor gives you a pack (all made up for practice): a week's copies of client receipts, card machine slips and supplier invoices; a bank deposit slip and a short bank statement; and a payroll sheet for three employees giving each one's gross pay and the amount of each deduction (PAYE income tax, NIS, NHT and Education Tax), plus the employer's share, as figures to use (not real rates). Give each member a lead task, and have another member check it: (1) sort all receipts and invoices by date and file them in a labelled folder; (2) record the week's sales and costs in a cash book; (3) total the cash book and check it against the bank deposit slip and statement, noting any difference; (4) prepare a payslip for each employee showing gross pay, each deduction and net pay; (5) prepare a payroll summary showing the total deductions and employer's share to be paid over to Tax Administration Jamaica; (6) list the three records the salon must keep from this week and say how and where they will be stored. Use a calculator and check every total twice. Photograph each stage and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: A records pack from the assessor (receipts, invoices, bank slip and statement, payroll sheet)
A blank cash book page and blank payslips
A labelled folder or box file, hole punch and dividers
A phone or camera for photos
photos: The receipts and invoices sorted by date
The completed cash book page with totals
The check against the bank slip and statement, with any difference noted
The labelled folder with the week's records filed
checklist: Sorted and filed documents in date order without losing any
Entered sales and costs in the cash book accurately
Totalled figures correctly and checked them twice
Checked the cash book against the bank records and explained any difference
Prepared payslips showing gross pay, each of the four deductions and the correct net pay
Prepared a correct payroll summary of the amounts to be paid over to TAJ
Kept the records neat, private and properly labelled
Checked another member's work and corrected mistakes politely
safety: Treat the pack as private business information; do not take photos of it outside the task
Use the hole punch and any stapler carefully, keeping fingers clear
Keep the work area tidy and the walkways clear
Use only the made-up names and figures in the pack; never use real personal or tax numbers
